pages.title: About
pages.content:
Yuzuriha Retreat opened in 2014 in a former forestry hostel at Larch Hill Lane 9 in Fernhollow Valley. Ines Calloway, a yoga teacher, took over the empty building with a borrowed van, twelve mats and a wood stove. In 2018 the old storage barn became the practice hall, fourteen metres by nine, with a timber floor and tall windows onto the larches.

The lodge has never grown past twelve guests, so that everyone sits at one long table and every guest is known by name by the first supper. We have eight rooms, four single and four twin, no televisions, and a basket by the door where phones rest during practice. We ask, and never enforce.

What we do not do

  • We make no promises about cures, detoxes or transformations.
  • We do not police screens or silence outside the quiet mornings of the Seven-Day Retreat.
  • We do not run ceremonies. We teach yoga, walk in the forest and cook plain meals.

Meet the seven people who run the lodge on the Teachers page.

pages.title: Calendar
pages.content:
Four retreats, twelve places each, eight dates in 2027. Every price includes all meals and all teaching, in a twin-shared room.

First Light, three days, €540

12–14 March · 23–25 April 2027. Morning and evening practice, two walks.

Forest, five days, €920

22–26 March · 10–14 May 2027. A full retreat day every day.

Quiet, seven days, €1,280

4–10 April · 6–12 June 2027. Silent mornings until lunch.

Weekend Walking, three days, €480

7–9 May · 18–20 June 2027. Three long walks and one practice a day.

Dates for July to November are published in the January letter. Reserve a place.

pages.title: A Retreat Day
pages.content:
Every retreat day runs on the same routine, from the bell to the quiet hours.

  • 05:45 · Wake bell, one bell in the corridor
  • 06:15 · Morning practice, 90 minutes, on the deck or in the hall
  • 08:00 · Breakfast at the long table
  • 10:00 · Forest walk, two to three hours: the 9 km larch ridge loop or the 5 km stream path
  • 12:30 · Lunch
  • 14:00 · Rest, reading, an optional workshop
  • 16:30 · Evening practice, 60 minutes, slow and restorative
  • 18:30 · Supper
  • 21:00 · Quiet hours until the bell

Arrival and departure

Arrival day: the lodge van leaves Fernhollow station at 14:30 (25 minutes), welcome tea is at 16:00 and the first supper at 18:30. Departure day: last practice at 06:15, brunch at 10:00 and the van to the station at 14:00.

pages.title: Retreats & Prices
pages.content:
Prices are per person in euros, with every meal and all teaching included, in a twin-shared room.

  • Three-Day First Light Retreat, 3 days, 2 nights: €540
  • Weekend Walking Retreat, 3 days, 2 nights: €480
  • Five-Day Forest Retreat, 5 days, 4 nights: €920
  • Seven-Day Quiet Retreat, 7 days, 6 nights: €1,280
  • Single room supplement, per night: €35
  • Private session, 60 minutes, with a booked retreat: €60
  • Whole-lodge hire for organisers, up to 12 guests, minimum 3 nights: €2,400 per night

A 30% deposit holds your place; the balance is due 30 days before arrival. The deposit is refunded in full until 45 days before arrival.

pages.title: Rooms
pages.content:
Eight rooms: four single, four twin. Each has linen, a wool blanket and a reading lamp, and none has a television. There are three shared bathrooms and a wood stove in the hall.

Two ground-floor rooms are step-free, and the covered deck can be reached by a ramp. The practice hall measures 14 × 9 m with a timber floor and holds twelve mats with room to spare.

pages.title: Kitchen
pages.content:
Mateo Ruiz cooks three plain meals a day: breakfast at 08:00, lunch at 12:30 and supper at 18:30, with tea at any hour. The food is vegetarian, with fish twice a week, and there is bread every day.

Tell us about dietary needs when you reserve. Vegan, gluten-free and nut-free meals are handled; there is one kitchen and no separate allergen kitchen.

pages.title: Teachers
pages.content:
Seven people run the lodge.

  • Ines Calloway, founder and yoga teacher: leads the morning practice.
  • Hana Lindgren, yoga teacher: the slow evening practice.
  • Sun-hee Park, meditation and breath: leads the Seven-Day Quiet Retreat.
  • Kofi Mensah, forest guide: the 9 km larch ridge loop and the stream path.
  • Mateo Ruiz, cook: three plain meals a day.
  • Nadia Haddad, house manager: answers every reservation.
  • Tomas Eklund, caretaker: drives the lodge van and keeps the wood stove.

pages.title: Getting Here
pages.content:
Larch Hill Lane 9, Fernhollow Valley. The lodge is open from March to November.

By train: the lodge van meets the afternoon train at Fernhollow station at 14:30 and takes 25 minutes; on departure day it leaves the lodge for the station at 14:00. By car: parking for eight cars, the last 2 km are gravel.

posts.title: Tea before practice
posts.excerpt: At 05:50 Ines boils the kettle and carries twelve cups to the deck before the bell.
posts.content:
The kettle goes on at ten to six. By then Ines has been up for twenty minutes: she has swept the deck, wiped the dew from the rail and counted twelve cups onto the long tray, one for every guest and none for herself. The bell is not until a quarter to six, but the tea is the part of the morning she will not hand to anyone else.

It began in the first season, 2014, when the lodge had one kettle that took eleven minutes to boil and a teacher who could not sleep. Ines carried the cups out because it was something to do with her hands. Guests came to the deck in their blankets and, without being asked, did not talk. Nobody has ever written that into the timetable, but the first cup is now the way the quiet begins.

The tea is plain: a loose green leaf from a grower in the next valley, water that has stopped boiling for a minute, nothing sweet. She pours it from the kettle into the row of cups along the deck rail and watches the steam go up into the fog below the larches. If it rains the cups move into the hall, to the low table by the wood stove.

There is a small ritual after it. Each guest takes their cup, finds a place on the boards and holds it with both hands until it is cool enough to drink. Nobody checks a phone; the phones are in the basket by the door. At 06:15 Ines walks to the front of the mats and the practice begins, and the empty cups are collected by whoever finishes first.

We are sometimes asked what we teach in the morning practice. The honest answer is that the tea is half of it. A body that has been given something warm to hold, in a cold place, with nothing to decide, tends to settle on its own. The yoga that follows is ninety slow minutes; the cup is the first five.

If you come for a First Light retreat, the cups will be waiting. Bring a wool layer, because the deck is cold before the sun reaches it, and arrive at the rail before the bell.

posts.title: Walking the larch ridge
posts.excerpt: Kofi’s nine kilometre loop, the halfway bench and the fog that lifts at eleven.
posts.content:
Kofi Mensah walks the larch ridge loop more often than anyone alive, and he still stops at the same four places. The loop is nine kilometres, leaves the lodge by the back gate at ten in the morning and takes between two and three hours, depending on the fog and on whoever is slowest. He insists that the slowest guest sets the pace.

The first stretch climbs gently through spruce, on a path softened by decades of needles. After forty minutes the trees change: the larches begin, tall and pale, and the light falls differently between them. In October they turn the colour of the lodge boards, and in March they are bare and silver. Kofi says the ridge has three seasons and a rumour of a fourth.

Halfway round, at the highest point, there is a wooden bench that Tomas built from a fallen beam in 2019. It faces the valley, which is usually full of fog at ten. The group sits for ten minutes without talking. Then the fog thins from the edges, as it nearly always does at about eleven, and the roofs of Fernhollow appear one at a time like something being remembered.

The return is downhill along the stream, past a footbridge that the guests have named the Slow Bridge because nobody crosses it quickly. Kofi carries a flask, a first-aid kit and a map he never opens. If anyone is tired there is a shorter way home of five kilometres by the stream path, and it is taken without comment and without any sense of having given up.

We do not walk to reach anything. The Forest and Weekend Walking retreats include several loops, and the walk is as much a part of the practice as the mats. Wear shoes you have already walked in, bring a water bottle, and expect to be back for lunch at 12:30.

posts.title: Supper at half past six
posts.excerpt: Mateo’s one-pot suppers and the bread that rises during the afternoon rest.
posts.content:
Supper is at half past six, and Mateo starts it at noon. The bread is the first job: he mixes the dough before lunch, leaves it to rise through the afternoon rest, and bakes it at five so that the loaf is still warm when it reaches the long table. Guests who nap on the deck sometimes wake to the smell and take it for a dream.

Everything else is one pot. A soup of beans and winter greens, or a stew of roasted roots with barley, or a dal that has been cooking since the walk began. Mateo cooks vegetarian food, with fish on two evenings a week, and the plates are never decorated. He says the point of supper is not to impress anyone but to end the day with something plain and warm.

The long table seats twelve, which is why the lodge has twelve guests. Bowls are passed from hand to hand, and the person nearest the kitchen door ladles. Nobody is asked to sit in a particular place; by the second evening people have chosen anyway and, by the fourth, are sitting beside different neighbours on purpose.

Conversation at supper is allowed, and during the Seven-Day Quiet Retreat it waits until after lunch. After the meal there is tea, and whoever has finished first helps to clear. The kitchen has one sink and one dishcloth, and there is a rota on the door written in Mateo’s small hand.

When you reserve, tell Nadia what you cannot eat. Vegan, gluten-free and nut-free suppers are cooked every week; there is one kitchen, so we cannot promise a kitchen free of every trace. The rest is plain: a bowl, a slice of bread, and the quiet hour that follows.
